items.claim: LSASS memory contains credential material generated by interactive, batch, and service logons; a dump is evidence only when the process memory was read and a credential artifact was recovered, not when a dump file is merely created.
items.body: After a successful logon, LSASS memory can contain credential material for the session. To test the finding, capture a memory dump from the LSASS process on the target, then recover a credential artifact for a named account and demonstrate its use. Record the dump source, the account whose material was recovered, and the authentication that used it. A dump file by itself is only a container and can be empty, encrypted, or produced from a protected process.
items.disproof: A dump file that yields no credential, or a dump attempt blocked by LSA protection, is not a credential-access finding. LSA protection exists specifically to stop nonprotected processes from reading LSASS memory, so a blocked read is the control working.

sources.quote: After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory.
On Windows 8.1 and later, added protection for the LSA is provided to prevent nonprotected processes from reading memory and injecting code.

items.claim: The SAM database stores local account credential material, and extracting it requires reading the SAM and SYSTEM registry hives or equivalent in-memory access on the host; a successful extraction is proven by recovered hashes, not by the presence of the files.
items.body: The SAM database holds local account records, and the SYSTEM hive supplies the boot key needed to decrypt the stored hashes. A tester with local administrator or SYSTEM access can export both hives, take them off-host, and recover the hashes. Record the host, the account whose hash was recovered, and a successful reuse or cracking result. A copied SAM file without the matching SYSTEM material is not yet an extraction.
items.disproof: A SAM or SYSTEM file that yields no usable hash is not a credential-access finding. The files can be present on every host; the finding requires successful decryption and a recovered credential.

sources.quote: The SAM is a database file that contains local accounts for the host, typically those found with the net user command.

By default, Windows credentials are validated against the Security Accounts Manager (SAM) database on the local computer, or against Active Directory on a domain-joined computer, through the Winlogon service.

items.claim: NTDS.dit contains the domain's directory credential material and is located on domain controllers; extracting it requires domain controller access or a directory replication right, and the finding is proven by recovered domain hashes rather than by a copy of the file alone.
items.body: NTDS.dit is the Active Directory database on a domain controller. Extraction can be local, through a volume shadow copy or an offline copy, or remote, through a directory replication right such as DCSync. Record the domain controller, the extraction path, the account whose hash was recovered, and a successful replay or cracking result. A copy of NTDS.dit without the matching registry material or a replication response is not yet a credential extraction.
items.disproof: A copied NTDS.dit file that yields no domain hashes is not a credential-access finding. The database is present on every domain controller; the finding requires a recovered credential or a demonstrated replication response.

sources.quote: By default, the NTDS file (NTDS.dit) is located in %SystemRoot%\NTDS\Ntds.dit of a domain controller.
All domain controllers in a domain participate in replication and contain a complete copy of all directory information for their domain.
